power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 2 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

info.title: Multiplying Bayes Factors Across Studies: Which Hypotheses Are We Testing?

text.text: Bayesian evidence synthesis (BES) is a method for evaluating the empirical support for a common theory across multiple studies.
In each study, the theory predicts a set of order constraints on the parameters of interest.
Evidence is aggregated by multiplying the Bayes factors of the individual studies, yielding the product Bayes factor (PBF).
The numerator of the PBF corresponds to the joint predicted hypothesis that the theory holds across different contexts, implying that the predicted order constraints are correct in each study.
Since the Bayes factor is a relative measure of evidence, interpreting the PBF requires a clear understanding of the alternative hypothesis.
The joint alternative is represented by the denominator of the PBF and states that the respective study-specific alternative hypothesis holds in each study.
However, this joint alternative may lack both a clear substantive interpretation and a theoretical justification.

We investigate how different combinations of study-specific alternative hypotheses give rise to distinct joint alternatives, focusing on three alternatives common in order-constrained inference: the null, the unconstrained, and the complement hypothesis.

In particular, we show that multiplying Bayes factors involving study-specific complements does not test the theory against its complement (i.e., the hypothesis that the theoretical predictions are false in at least one study).
Finally, we provide recommendations for specifying meaningful joint alternative hypotheses that support a clear interpretation of BES results and are useful for theory testing.
A central goal of science is to test theories that assume relationships between latent constructs.
Because constructs are by definition unobservable, testing a theory requires researchers to rely on specific operationalizations (Stroebe & Strack, 2014).
text.formatted: Because constructs are by definition unobservable, testing a theory requires researchers to rely on specific operationalizations <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Stroebe & Strack, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: However, since a theory makes claims about the constructs, not about a particular operationalization, its predictions should hold regardless of how the constructs are operationalized.
For example, dual-process theories of persuasion (Chaiken, 1980) posit, among other things, that deeper processing of a message increases the impact of argument quality on persuasion.
text.formatted: For example, dual-process theories of persuasion <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Chaiken, 1980)</ref> posit, among other things, that deeper processing of a message increases the impact of argument quality on persuasion.

text.text: If the theory is correct, it should not matter whether processing depth is manipulated through personal relevance (Petty et al., 1981) or through the expectation to discuss the message later (Chaiken, 1980).
text.formatted: If the theory is correct, it should not matter whether processing depth is manipulated through personal relevance <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Petty et al., 1981)</ref> or through the expectation to discuss the message later <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Chaiken, 1980)</ref>.

text.text: As Baribault et al. (2018 Baribault et al. ( , p. 2608) put it, "theoretical statements made by researchers almost without fail imply some degree of robustness to irrelevant variables".
text.formatted: As <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Baribault et al. (2018</ref> <ref type="bibr">Baribault et al. ( , p. 2608</ref>) put it, "theoretical statements made by researchers almost without fail imply some degree of robustness to irrelevant variables".

text.text: When researchers intentionally vary theoretically irrelevant aspects of a study while testing the same theory, they perform a conceptual replication (Schmidt, 2009).
text.formatted: When researchers intentionally vary theoretically irrelevant aspects of a study while testing the same theory, they perform a conceptual replication <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Schmidt, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Besides varying operationalizations, conceptual replications may differ in participant populations, experimental procedures, statistical analyses, or other aspects of the study design, such as timing and number of measurement occasions.

When a theory is supported across different constellations of theoretically irrelevant variables, our confidence in it increases because the proposed relationships generalize across contexts (Lakens, 2022; Schmidt, 2009; Stroebe & Strack, 2014).
text.formatted: When a theory is supported across different constellations of theoretically irrelevant variables, our confidence in it increases because the proposed relationships generalize across contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Lakens, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Schmidt, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Stroebe & Strack, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, it is often of interest to synthesize evidence for or against a theory across a set of conceptual replications.
Yet the very heterogeneity that gives conceptual replications higher evidential value poses challenges for statistical analysis.

For example, Bayesian sequential updating (Scheibehenne et al., 2016; Schönbrodt et al., 2017) pools the raw data across all studies, which requires all studies to share the same data format and model structure.
text.formatted: For example, Bayesian sequential updating <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Scheibehenne et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Schönbrodt et al., 2017)</ref> pools the raw data across all studies, which requires all studies to share the same data format and model structure.

text.text: This makes Bayesian sequential updating suitable for evidence synthesis across direct, but not conceptual, replications.
In comparison, standard meta-analysis approaches are more flexible because aggregation occurs at the level of effect sizes.
Specifically, random-effects meta-analysis assumes between-study heterogeneity and allows the true effect size to vary across studies.

However, conventional meta-analysis may also not be suitable for synthesizing conceptual replications because it assumes that study-specific effect sizes are expressed in a common metric (e.g., Cohen's d) and are thus comparable (Borenstein et al., 2010).
text.formatted: However, conventional meta-analysis may also not be suitable for synthesizing conceptual replications because it assumes that study-specific effect sizes are expressed in a common metric (e.g., Cohen's d) and are thus comparable <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Borenstein et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: For conceptual replications, this assumption is usually violated for two reasons.
First, different studies often test different predictions derived from the same theory.
For example, the first study may examine a simple mean difference, the second a complex interaction, and the third a specific ordering of regression coefficients.
The studies thus involve different parameters-sometimes multiple-that cannot be reduced to a single effect size.
Moreover, even if each study yields exactly one effect size, it is unlikely that all studies use the same measure.

And although different effect sizes can sometimes be converted into a common metric, such transformations can introduce "strong or even untenable assumptions, resulting in estimates of effect sizes with unknown distributional properties" (Van Assen et al., 2023, p. 1).
text.formatted: And although different effect sizes can sometimes be converted into a common metric, such transformations can introduce "strong or even untenable assumptions, resulting in estimates of effect sizes with unknown distributional properties" <ref type="bibr">(Van Assen et al., 2023, p. 1)</ref>.

text.text: Second, even if all studies test the same hypothesis with identical designs and statistical methods, effect-size comparability can be violated, for example, when each study controls for a different set of covariates (Van Lissa et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Second, even if all studies test the same hypothesis with identical designs and statistical methods, effect-size comparability can be violated, for example, when each study controls for a different set of covariates <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Van Lissa et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Bayesian evidence synthesis (BES; Kuiper et al., 2013) addresses the limitations of existing synthesis methods by accommodating between-study heterogeneity in hypotheses, study designs, and statistical methods. 1 BES requires that each study test at least one theory-derived hypothesis and that the evidence for these study-specific hypotheses be quantified by a Bayes factor (BF).
text.formatted: Bayesian evidence synthesis (BES; <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Kuiper et al., 2013)</ref> addresses the limitations of existing synthesis methods by accommodating between-study heterogeneity in hypotheses, study designs, and statistical methods. <ref type="foot" target="#foot_0">1</ref> BES requires that each study test at least one theory-derived hypothesis and that the evidence for these study-specific hypotheses be quantified by a Bayes factor (BF).

text.text: The core idea of BES is straightforward: The study-specific Bayes factors are multiplied to obtain the product Bayes factor (PBF).
The PBF quantifies the evidence that all studies together provide for the underlying theory.

The two main assumptions of BES are that (1) all studies test the same underlying theory and (2) each study provides independent evidence, which requires that the study-specific hypotheses, data, and prior distributions be independent across studies (see Section 3.1).

BES has intuitive appeal and has been applied to a range of empirical studies, for example, to synthesize evidence on the effect of parental age on offspring mental health (Zondervan-Zwijnenburg, Veldkamp, et al., 2020), the development of self-control during adolescence (Zondervan-Zwijnenburg, Richards, et al., 2020), and differences in informants' ratings of children's self-control (Kevenaar et al., 2021).
text.formatted: BES has intuitive appeal and has been applied to a range of empirical studies, for example, to synthesize evidence on the effect of parental age on offspring mental health <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Zondervan-Zwijnenburg, Veldkamp, et al., 2020)</ref>, the development of self-control during adolescence <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Zondervan-Zwijnenburg, Richards, et al., 2020)</ref>, and differences in informants' ratings of children's self-control <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Kevenaar et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: However, previous applications of BES also reveal an important blind spot.
Since BES rests on computing the PBF, the interpretation of its results inherits a key property of Bayesian model selection, namely, that evidence is relative.
The Bayes factor does not test a hypothesis in an absolute sense but rather quantifies the evidence for one hypothesis relative to another (Tendeiro & Kiers, 2019).
text.formatted: The Bayes factor does not test a hypothesis in an absolute sense but rather quantifies the evidence for one hypothesis relative to another <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Tendeiro & Kiers, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, a correct interpretation of the PBF requires specifying a clear competing hypothesis against which the theory is evaluated.
However, previous applications of BES have often not specified this hypothesis explicitly, which increases the risk of misinterpreting the results.
The present paper makes four main contributions.
First, we clarify which joint hypotheses are being tested when multiplying study-specific Bayes factors.

Second, we show how different combinations of study-specific alternative hypotheses give rise to different joint alternative hypotheses, and demonstrate that these choices can substantially affect conclusions about the combined evidence for a theory.
Third, we show that multiplying Bayes factors against the study-specific complements does not yield a test of the theory against its complement.
We call the latter the complete complement and derive the computation of the Bayes factor against it from the study-specific Bayes factors alone.
Finally, we provide recommendations on specifying joint alternative hypotheses that are meaningful in the context of theory testing.
In BES, one first needs to select a set of studies, each of which is regarded as an independent test of the theory of interest.
For each study t, a study-specific predicted hypothesis is derived from the theory:

In mathematical psychology, many theories can be translated into informative statistical hypotheses that encode substantive expectations about the observed outcomes or model parameters (Heck & Davis-Stober, 2019; Heck et al., 2023).
text.formatted: In mathematical psychology, many theories can be translated into informative statistical hypotheses that encode substantive expectations about the observed outcomes or model parameters <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Heck & Davis-Stober, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Heck et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Informative statistical hypotheses are formally defined by restricting the parameters θ of a statistical model via a set of equality constraints (e.g., θ1 = θ 2 ), order constraints (e.g., θ1 ≤ θ 2 ), and/or interval constraints (e.g., -0.1 ≤ θ1 ≤ 0.1).
BES assumes that the theory implies such a predicted statistical hypothesis for each study.
To illustrate BES, we introduce two running examples: order constraints on choice probabilities and interval constraints in equivalence testing.
Suppose we want to evaluate the evidence for the existence of precognition, defined by Bem (2011, p. 410) as "accessing information yet to be determined in the future".
text.formatted: Suppose we want to evaluate the evidence for the existence of precognition, defined by <ref type="bibr">Bem (2011, p. 410)</ref> as "accessing information yet to be determined in the future".

text.text: Experiment 1 by Bem (2011) investigated precognition for positively valenced stimuli by showing participants two images of curtains on a display, one with a picture behind it and the other with blank space.
text.formatted: Experiment 1 by <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Bem (2011)</ref> investigated precognition for positively valenced stimuli by showing participants two images of curtains on a display, one with a picture behind it and the other with blank space.

text.text: Participants were asked to select the curtain behind which they believed the picture to be.
The location of the images was randomly determined after the participant had made their decision.

In this experiment, the positively valenced stimuli were erotic images, and Bem hypothesized that "participants would be able to identify the position of the hidden erotic picture significantly more often than chance (50%)" (Bem, 2011, p. 409).
text.formatted: In this experiment, the positively valenced stimuli were erotic images, and Bem hypothesized that "participants would be able to identify the position of the hidden erotic picture significantly more often than chance (50%)" <ref type="bibr">(Bem, 2011, p. 409)</ref>.

text.text: Suppose that we want to analyze the data of three replication studies of Bem's Experiment 1.
Based on the theoretical assumption that people have precognition for positive stimuli, we derive the same study-specific informative hypothesis for the hit rate θ (t) in all studies:
The left panel of Figure 1 illustrates the study-specific hypotheses for each of the three replication studies in pink.

text.text: In this example, BES could answer the research question: How much evidence do the three replication studies jointly provide in favor of precognition for positive stimuli?
Equivalence testing aims to assess whether an observed effect is "too small to be meaningful" (Lakens, 2022), rather than whether it differs from the absolute null of no effect.
text.formatted: Equivalence testing aims to assess whether an observed effect is "too small to be meaningful" <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Lakens, 2022)</ref>, rather than whether it differs from the absolute null of no effect.

text.text: This is realized by specifying an informative hypothesis that covers a region around an effect size of zero (i.e., no difference in means).
If the observed effect falls into this region, it is considered too small to be meaningful, and statistical equivalence is inferred.

Example B highlights a key strength of BES, namely, that it allows researchers to synthesize studies that test different predicted hypotheses derived from the same theory.
Here, the predicted hypotheses specify different equivalence intervals and concern different effect sizes-a between-person and a within-person mean difference.
In principle, BES can accommodate even more complex cases, such as studies with multiple parameters or structurally different types of constraints.
Bayes factors always compare two hypotheses against each other.
In BES, in each study, the predicted hypothesis H 1 is tested against a competing alternative hypothesis H a by computing the study-specific Bayes factor where (t) are the data observed in study t.

The most common alternative for the predicted H 1 is the null hypothesis H 0 , which either fixes the testrelevant parameters to a specific value (e.g., θ = 0) or constrains different parameters to be equal (e.g., θ1 = θ 2 ).

The null generally reflects the expectation that there is no effect at all. 2 In turn, the unconstrained hypothesis H u imposes no constraints on the parameters at all, allowing them to vary freely over the entire parameter space, which makes it a maximally uninformative hypothesis.

This joint predicted hypothesis formally combines all study-specific predicted hypotheses with the logical AND operator, and is defined on the parameter vector that concatenates the study-specific parameters θ (t) , θ = θ (1) , θ (2) , . . . , θ (T ) , where the parameters can be thought of as separate dimensions (indexed per study t) of an overarching joint model across all studies.

According to probability theory, simple multiplication is the appropriate operation under three conditions, which must hold for the predicted and the alternative hypotheses alike.
First, each study tests a separate hypothesis, meaning that its order and equality constraints concern only its own parameters θ (t) and not those of other studies.
In this case, the joint hypothesis corresponds to the Cartesian product of the study-specific hypotheses, 1 .
Second, the data are conditionally independent across studies given the parameters, t) ).
Third, the prior distributions of the study-specific parameters are independent between studies.
Under these assumptions, the joint Bayes factor equals the product of the studyspecific Bayes factors.

text.text: Because BF (joint) 1,a pits the joint predicted hypothesis against a joint alternative, its correct interpretation depends on which alternative hypothesis is specified.

If each study tests the predicted hypothesis against a point null alternative, the resulting joint Bayes factor BF (joint) 1,0 can be interpreted as the relative evidence that the theory holds in each individual study compared to the effect being absent in each study.
If we test against the unconstrained hypothesis, then BF (joint) 1,u pits the joint H 1 against all possibilities of parameter combinations across studies.
The joint Bayes factor can then be interpreted as relative evidence that the theory holds in each individual study compared to not having any theoretical account for the data.
Framed differently, BF (joint) 1,u quantifies the degree to which imposing the theoretical constraints improves our predictions of the data as compared to not making any predictions at all.

The weights π Ω are the prior probabilities of the individual components H Ω under the assumption that the complete complement holds, that is, that the predictions fail in at least one study.
These weights express how plausible each pattern of successful and failed predictions across studies is considered a priori, excluding the pattern in which all predictions succeed.
There are two natural choices for the weights.

Complexity weighting assigns each component a weight equal to its share of the prior mass of the complete complement, where c Ω is the complexity of the component H Ω and c (t) 1 the complexity of the predicted hypothesis in study t.
This corresponds to restricting the encompassing prior to the complete complement.

text.text: In contrast, under complexity weighting, the complete complement expects failed predictions primarily in those studies with predicted hypotheses of low complexity (i.e., hypotheses that cover only a small part of the prior), so that evidence against these predictions counts more strongly.

For instance, consider two studies whose predicted hypotheses have complexities c1 = 0.10 and c1 = 0.50, and assume that one of them yields BF 1,c = 1/3, whereas the other provides no evidence (BF 1,c = 1).
Under equal weighting, BF (joint) 1,c * = 3/7 ≈ 0.43, regardless of which study provides the evidence.
Under complexity weighting, the joint Bayes factor is 0.35 if the evidence comes from the study with c1 = 0.10 but 0.49 if it comes from the study with c1 = 0.50.

The asymmetric impact of studies on BF (joint) 1,c * under complexity weighting is defensible if all studies concern the same parameter on the same scale, because a narrower predicted hypothesis then represents a more precise, and hence riskier, prediction.
In BES, however, studies often concern different parameters with different ranges, so that differences in complexity need not reflect differences in how precisely the theory is tested.
For instance, in Example B, the equivalence intervals differ only because one grade point corresponds to a different number of percentage points in each study's grading system.

With the same prior on the mean difference in all three studies, Study 1 would have the smallest complexity, and so complexity weighting would treat it as the most likely site of falsification and let evidence against its prediction count most strongly.
Yet there is no substantive reason why a failed prediction in Study 1 should weigh more heavily against the theory than a failed prediction in Study 3.
Equal weighting avoids such asymmetries.
So far, we have assumed that each study tests a single predicted hypothesis.
However, in some applications, the individual studies may also test multiple competing predicted hypotheses (e.g., qualitatively different sets of order constraints on the parameters).
BES can also be applied in these cases, provided that all studies test the same competing theoretical accounts, so that each joint predicted hypothesis represents a substantive theoretical claim.
As in the single-hypothesis case, multiplying the study-specific Bayes factors for one of the predicted hypotheses against its complement does not yield a test against the complete complement.

Unlike in that case, however, Steps 1 to 3 need to be adapted, because the parameter space of each study is now partitioned into more than two regions, namely, the predicted hypotheses and the complement of their union.

To compare multiple joint predicted hypotheses simultaneously (e.g., via posterior model probabilities), the complete complement of each joint predicted hypothesis is unsuitable, because it contains the other joint predicted hypotheses.
Instead, it is more useful to define a single complete complement as the remainder of the joint parameter space once all joint predicted hypotheses are removed (i.e., the complement of their union).
It comprises all combinations of study-specific hypotheses in which no single predicted hypothesis holds across all studies.

That is, the data are somewhat more likely if the predictions fail in at least one experiment than if they hold throughout.

Notably, testing against the joint unconstrained hypothesis yields a virtually identical value, BF (joint) 1,u = 0.36. Volker et al. (2022) investigated the effects of network embeddedness on trust and cooperation.

text.text: Network embeddedness occurs when a person X can access information from third parties about their previous interactions with person Y. The authors tested the overarching hypothesis that network embeddedness promotes trust and cooperation by synthesizing evidence across eight heterogeneous studies.

For example, network embeddedness was compared either with no embeddedness or with dyadic embeddedness, in which X can draw upon previous experiences with Y to guide the decision of how much-or whether-to trust them in a current exchange.

The studies also used different games (e.g., trust game, prisoner's dilemma, investment game) and measured different outcomes (trustfulness, trustworthiness, or cooperation).  3 presents the study-specific Bayes factors reported by the authors, together with the joint Bayes factors that we computed from them.

Likewise, testing against the complete joint complement supports the joint predicted hypothesis, though with substantially weaker evidence, BF (joint) 1,c * = 7.24.
Again, we observe that the Bayes factor testing against the complete complement is virtually identical to that obtained from testing against the joint unconstrained hypothesis, BF (joint) 1,u = 7.24.
We showed that the conclusions drawn from Bayesian evidence synthesis (Klugkist & Volker, 2025; Kuiper et al., 2013) depend on the joint alternative hypothesis against which the theory is evaluated.
text.formatted: We showed that the conclusions drawn from Bayesian evidence synthesis <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Klugkist & Volker, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Kuiper et al., 2013)</ref> depend on the joint alternative hypothesis against which the theory is evaluated.

text.text: We considered four joint alternative hypotheses: the null, the unconstrained, the incomplete complement, and the complete complement.
Among these, we argued that the incomplete joint complement is of limited relevance for theory testing because it rarely represents a substantively interesting claim.

Multiplying study-specific Bayes factors that test theoretically derived order constraints against their complements implicitly pits the theory against the incomplete joint complement, which states that the theoretical predictions are wrong in every study.

For theory testing, the complete joint complement is more appropriate, because it states that the predictions are wrong in at least one study, that is, that the theory does not hold across all studies.
We showed how the Bayes factor against the complete complement can be computed from the same study-specific Bayes factors that are multiplied in standard BES.

Importantly, the choice between the incomplete and the complete joint complement matters in practice: In our empirical examples, they led to substantially different-in one case even opposite-conclusions about the theory.

The discrepancy between the two types of complements is also reflected in the geometry of the joint parameter space.
For more than one study, the incomplete complement is a strict subset of the complete complement.
As studies are added, the former shrinks exponentially, whereas the latter approaches the entire parameter space.

In Example A (Section 2.2.1), the two complements coincide for a single study, each covering 50% of the parameter space; for two studies, they cover 25% and 75%, and for three studies, 12.5% and 87.5%, respectively.

Put differently, the complete complement has a higher complexity, meaning that, under the encompassing prior, the parameters are a priori more likely to fall within the complete complement than the incomplete complement (Klugkist & Hoijtink, 2007).
text.formatted: Put differently, the complete complement has a higher complexity, meaning that, under the encompassing prior, the parameters are a priori more likely to fall within the complete complement than the incomplete complement <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Klugkist & Hoijtink, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Setting aside the incomplete joint complement, we argue that there is no universally correct choice among the remaining three joint alternatives.
Which alternative hypothesis is appropriate depends on the scientific question.

The joint null is appropriate when the question is whether an effect is present in all studies or absent in all studies, for example, in clinical trials, where it provides a clear benchmark for concluding that a treatment has no effect.
However, neither the joint null nor the joint predicted hypothesis covers more complex scenarios in which the effect is present in some studies but absent in others.
In such cases, BF (joint) 1,0 necessarily contrasts two false hypotheses, so that whichever hypothesis is favored by the Bayes factor, the conclusion is misleading.

Moreover, testing against the joint null is subject to an asymmetry: Since Bayes factors based on commonly used alternative priors accumulate evidence against a false point null much faster than evidence for a true one (Johnson & Rossell, 2010), the few studies in which the effect is present can provide overwhelming support for the predictions that outweighs the comparatively weak evidence for the null from the remaining studies.
text.formatted: Moreover, testing against the joint null is subject to an asymmetry: Since Bayes factors based on commonly used alternative priors accumulate evidence against a false point null much faster than evidence for a true one <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Johnson & Rossell, 2010)</ref>, the few studies in which the effect is present can provide overwhelming support for the predictions that outweighs the comparatively weak evidence for the null from the remaining studies.

text.text: Contrasting two false hypotheses cannot occur when testing against the complete complement or the joint unconstrained hypothesis.

In both cases, the predicted and the alternative hypotheses are exhaustive together, meaning that every possible combination of parameter values across studies is covered by at least one of them: H (joint) u covers the entire joint parameter space on its own, and H (joint) c * covers exactly the part that H (joint) 1 leaves out.
Therefore, if the statistical model itself is correctly specified, then at least one of the two compared hypotheses is true, even when the predictions hold in some studies but fail in others.
This protects against favoring a false joint predicted hypothesis merely because the alternative is even further from the truth.

In cognitive modeling, this protection is achieved by including a saturated model as a "catch all" alternative, which leaves the choice probabilities unconstrained and can therefore accommodate any data pattern (Lee, 2016).
text.formatted: In cognitive modeling, this protection is achieved by including a saturated model as a "catch all" alternative, which leaves the choice probabilities unconstrained and can therefore accommodate any data pattern <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Lee, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Since all substantive models are nested within it, the saturated model corresponds to the encompassing model in Bayesian tests of order constraints, that is, to the unconstrained hypothesis (Heck et al., 2017). 6 A substantive model is then selected only if it accounts for the data better than the saturated model, which protects against selecting models that do not fit the data in absolute terms (Heck et al., 2017).

text.text: The complete complement offers the same protection without overlapping with H (joint) 1 , because it accommodates every pattern that the predictions rule out.
In contrast, neither the joint null nor the incomplete joint complement offers such protection, since neither covers mixed patterns.
The unconstrained hypothesis has often been used as the alternative when testing order constraints (e.g., Heck & Davis-Stober, 2019; Hoijtink, 2012; Zwilling et al., 2019).

text.text: Two objections follow on this basis, but we argue that neither disqualifies H (joint) u in the context of theory testing.

First, the comparison of the competing models is said to lack a clear qualitative contrast: Whether a parameter falls above or below a certain boundary cannot be answered for values in the shared region and is better addressed by comparing disjoint regions of the parameter space (Shiffrin et al., 2016).
text.formatted: First, the comparison of the competing models is said to lack a clear qualitative contrast: Whether a parameter falls above or below a certain boundary cannot be answered for values in the shared region and is better addressed by comparing disjoint regions of the parameter space <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Shiffrin et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: We agree that directional questions require disjoint hypotheses, which are obtained in BES by using the complete complement.
If each study is an independent test of the theory, the theory implies that its predictions hold in all studies, so that a violation in any single study counts against the theory.

By stating that the predictions fail in at least one study, the complete complement thus asks whether the theory makes any incorrect prediction, which makes it the natural choice for exposing a theory to falsification attempts.

However, the comparison against H (joint) u addresses a different question, namely, whether committing to the theoretical predictions improves on making no predictions at all, which is the rationale underlying the encompassing Bayes factor (Hoijtink, 2012; Klugkist & Hoijtink, 2007).
text.formatted: However, the comparison against H (joint) u addresses a different question, namely, whether committing to the theoretical predictions improves on making no predictions at all, which is the rationale underlying the encompassing Bayes factor <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Hoijtink, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Klugkist & Hoijtink, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Here, the relevant competitor is not the failure of the theory but theoretical agnosticism, and the contrast between committing to the predictions and remaining agnostic is itself a qualitative one.
For this question, the overlap between the predicted and the unconstrained hypothesis is not incidental but constitutive:
The comparison is informative precisely because H 1 is a restriction of H u.
Second, because H 1 is nested in H u , the attainable evidence in favor of the predictions is necessarily bounded.

The bound thus quickly ceases to be a practical constraint as studies accumulate.

text.text: We have shown that one should be careful when multiplying Bayes factors across studies.
When doing so, one may inadvertently test the theory of interest against a competing hypothesis that does not reflect a theoretically relevant position.
As in any application of Bayes factors, researchers should carefully specify the hypotheses they compare (Heck et al., 2023; Tendeiro & Kiers, 2019).
text.formatted: As in any application of Bayes factors, researchers should carefully specify the hypotheses they compare <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Heck et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Tendeiro & Kiers, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: In Bayesian evidence synthesis, it is sensible to test one's predictions not only against the joint null hypothesis, but also against hypotheses that allow for heterogeneity across studies (i.e., for the predictions to hold in some studies but fail in others), such as the complete complement or the unconstrained hypothesis.

Whichever alternative is chosen, we recommend reporting the joint Bayes factor alongside the study-specific Bayes factors from which it was computed, so that readers can judge to what extent the aggregate reflects a consistent pattern of evidence.

However, in this third case, the joint Bayes factor is difficult to interpret.
A tempting misinterpretation is that BF (joint) 1,c quantifies the relative evidence for the set of theoretical predictions versus its complement.
This interpretation is incorrect because the conjunction of the study-specific complements does not form the complement of H (joint) 1 in the multidimensional parameter space.

The mismatch is immediately visible in Panels b and e of Figure 2: Outside the pink cuboids representing H (joint) 1 , large regions of the parameter space are not covered by the green cuboids representing H (joint) c .
The joint alternative that arises from multiplying the study-specific BF (t) 1,c is thus an incomplete complement of the theory.
Correctly interpreted, BF (joint) 1,c quantifies the relative evidence that the theoretical predictions hold in every study versus that they are false in every study.
Yet the latter claim is rarely of substantive interest, because a theory is already called into question if its predictions fail in a single study.
Testing the theory against its complement, and thus exposing it to falsification, therefore requires the complete complement.
The complete complement of H (joint) 1 covers all combinations of parameter values except those covered by H (joint) 1 .

It therefore includes the incomplete complement as the extreme case in which every study-specific complement is true, but also many other combinations, such as H (t) 1 holding in only one or two studies and H (t) c in the remaining ones.
In other words, the complete complement states that the theoretical predictions are false in at least one study.
Geometrically, it corresponds to the entire joint parameter space minus the joint predicted hypothesis (pink region), as shown in Panels c and f of Figure 2.

Since the two Bayes factors were virtually identical in our empirical examples and the alternatives cover increasingly similar regions of the parameter space as studies are added, one may expect the Bayes factors to converge.
However, their ratio, BF c * ,u , need not approach one as the number of studies grows.

Whether the two Bayes factors converge depends on the weighting of the components of the complete complement (i.e., the a priori plausibility of different patterns of correct and incorrect predictions across studies) and on the evidence provided by the studies (for details and derivations, see Section S1 of the Supplementary Material).
Under complexity weighting, the two Bayes factors always point in the same direction, with BF (joint) 1,c * at least as extreme as BF (joint) 1,u .
Moreover, their ratio approaches one as studies are added, unless the posterior concentrates in the joint predicted hypothesis.
In contrast, under equal weighting, which we consider more appropriate for theory testing (Section 5.4), neither property holds in general.

Depending on the complexities and the evidence, BF * can differ by several orders of magnitude even when many studies are synthesized, and may even point in opposite directions.The complexities and the evidence also explain why the two Bayes factors agreed in our empirical examples.
First, all predicted hypotheses had a complexity of 50% (i.e., c (t)1 = 0.50), so that all components of the joint parameter space had the same prior mass.
Equal weighting therefore weighted the components of the complete complement in the same way as the unconstrained hypothesis does.
As a result, the complete complement differed from the unconstrained hypothesis only in that it excluded the joint predicted hypothesis.

Second, because this excluded region received almost none of the prior and posterior probability (prior: 2 -7 ≈ 0.8% and 2 -16 < 0.01%; posterior: about 0.3% and 0.01%), the two Bayes factors agreed: The complete complement contained more than 99% of both the prior and the posterior mass of the unconstrained hypothesis, so that 7 For less precise predicted hypotheses (c (t) 1 > 0.50), the bound grows more slowly.

The contrast is even starker for the complement.
Although the study-specific BF (t) 1,c range from 0.02 to 75.34, the joint Bayes factor is BF (joint) 1,c * = 0.36.
Likewise, in the network-embeddedness example, the BF (t) 1,c range from 0.05 to 2.60 × 10 4 , whereas BF (joint)1,c * = 7.24 indicates moderate evidence.
The joint Bayes factor can thus mask effect heterogeneity that shows up as strong evidence in both directions at the study level.
Moreover, the joint Bayes factor need not favor the hypothesis supported by most studies, because it depends not only on the direction but also on the magnitude of the study-specific Bayes factors.
This was the case in the towel-reuse example: BF * both favored their respective alternatives, while only two of the seven individual experiments did.
However, these issues reflect a general limitation of any single summary measure of evidence.

As a remedy, researchers should inspect the distribution of study-specific Bayes factors alongside the joint Bayes factor, for example, in a histogram of the study-specific log BF values (for examples with heterogeneous person-specific Bayes factors, seeStephan et al., 2009).

We use "BES" to refer to the evidence synthesis method of multiplying Bayes factors across studies (e.g.,Kevenaar et al., 2021;Klugkist & Volker, 2025), rather than to Bayesian meta-analytic methods in general (e.g.,Mulder & Van Aert, 2026; Scheibehenne et al., 2016).

text.text: Unlike null-hypothesis significance testing, where the null is tested against "the alternative" (here, H1), we follow the BES literature in treating the null as one type of alternative to the predicted hypothesis.

text.text: An unconstrained hypothesis leaves the parameters of a given model free, whereas a saturated model can reproduce any data exactly.
text.formatted: An unconstrained hypothesis leaves the parameters of a given model free, whereas a saturated model can reproduce any data exactly.

text.text: Thus, every saturated model is unconstrained, but not every unconstrained model is saturated: In linear regression, for instance, the hypothesis β ∈ R is unconstrained, yet every value of β still implies a linear relationship, so that data following a nonlinear relationship cannot be reproduced.
The two coincide for binomial or multinomial models, as in the towel-reuse example, because then the parameters are the cell probabilities, each of which can match any observed relative frequency.
